summary: Gives a new Bidi rule for IDNA labels, to handle problems found when right-to-left scripts such as Arabic and Hebrew are used in internationalized domain names. It improves on shortcomings in the 2003 Bidi criterion. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Some languages are written from right to left, and computers reorder mixed-direction text to display it. This document sets out a checklist for right-to-left domain name labels, so that a label cannot be shown to a reader in a way that misleads them about which characters belong to which part of the name.

questions: why was the idna2003 bidi rule changed
subtitle: The six-part rule that decides which right-to-left domain labels are safe to display in IDNA2008.

tldr.problem: The 2003 IDNA Bidi criterion banned many valid words in right-to-left scripts, and for Dhivehi it banned every word, because labels there end in a combining mark.
tldr.mechanism: A new Bidi rule of six conditions checks the first character, the allowed character classes and the last character of each label, and keeps European and Arabic digits from mixing in one right-to-left label.
tldr.outcome: The rule is part of the revised IDNA protocol. Most labels allowed before are still allowed, so the operational impact is described as limited.

today: RFC 5893 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating document, so it remains the Bidi rule of the revised IDNA protocol, and only its Section 1.4 and Section 2 carry requirements.

sections.title: Purpose and Background
sections.content:
The purpose of this document is to establish a rule that can be applied to IDN labels in Unicode form, called U-labels, containing characters from scripts that are written from right to left. It is part of the revised IDNA protocol RFC 5891. When labels satisfy the rule, and when certain other conditions are satisfied, there is only a minimal chance of these labels being displayed in a confusing way by the Unicode bidirectional display algorithm. The other normative documents in the IDNA2008 document set establish criteria for valid labels, including listing the permitted characters; this document establishes additional validity criteria for labels in scripts normally written from right to left, and is not intended to place any requirements on domain names that do not contain characters from such scripts.

The Stringprep specification RFC 3454, part of IDNA2003, stated that if a string contains any RandALCat character, a RandALCat character MUST be the first character of the string and a RandALCat character MUST be the last character of the string. A RandALCat character is one with unambiguously right-to-left directionality.

The reasoning behind that prohibition was to ensure that every component of a displayed domain name has an unambiguously preferred direction. However, this made certain words in languages written with right-to-left scripts invalid as IDN labels, and in at least one case, Dhivehi, it meant that all the words of an entire language were forbidden as IDN labels. RFC 3454 did not explicitly state the requirement to be fulfilled, so it is impossible to determine whether a simple relaxation of the rule would continue to fulfil the requirement.

While this document specifies rules quite different from RFC 3454, most reasonable labels that were allowed under RFC 3454 will also be allowed under this specification. The most important examples of labels that become non-permitted are labels that mix Arabic and European digits inside a right-to-left label, and labels that use Arabic digits in a left-to-right label. The operational impact of using the new rule in the updated IDNA specification is therefore limited.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rule said a right-to-left label had to start and end with a plain right-to-left letter. That sounds tidy, but many right-to-left languages write their vowels and some of their final consonants as marks attached to the letters, so the last character of the label is a mark rather than a letter. Under the old rule, whole languages became unusable in domain names.

sections.title: Bidi Classes, Labels and Direction
sections.content:
The Unicode Standard specifies a Bidi property for each character, and that property controls the character's behaviour in the Unicode bidirectional algorithm. The values are L for left to right, which covers most letters in left-to-right scripts; R for right to left, most letters in non-Arabic right-to-left scripts; AL for Arabic letters; EN for European Number; ES for European Number Separator; ET for European Number Terminator; AN for Arabic Number; CS for Common Number Separator; NSM for Nonspacing Mark, which covers most combining accents; BN for Boundary Neutral; B for Paragraph Separator; S for Segment Separator; WS for Whitespace; and ON for Other Neutrals. The directional control characters LRE, LRO, RLE, RLO and PDF are not used in IDNA labels.

The document uses network order for the sequence of characters as transmitted on the wire or stored in a file, and display order for the sequence as imaged on a display. An RTL label is a label that contains at least one character of type R, AL or AN, and an LTR label is any label that is not an RTL label. A Bidi domain name is a domain name that contains at least one RTL label, which includes domain names containing only dots and right-to-left characters.
sections.plainLanguage: Every character in Unicode carries a small label saying which direction it leans: a plain left-to-right letter, a right-to-left letter, an Arabic letter, a European digit, an Arabic digit, a combining mark and so on. The rule in this document works entirely with those labels, never with the individual characters themselves.

sections.title: The Bidi Rule
sections.content:
The rule consists of six conditions and applies to labels in Bidi domain names. All of the conditions must be satisfied for the rule to be satisfied.

First, the first character must be a character with Bidi property L, R or AL. If it has the R or AL property it is an RTL label; if it has the L property it is an LTR label. Second, in an RTL label, only characters with the Bidi properties R, AL, AN, EN, ES, CS, ET, ON, BN or NSM are allowed. Third, in an RTL label, the end of the label must be a character with Bidi property R, AL, EN or AN, followed by zero or more characters with Bidi property NSM.

Fourth, in an RTL label, if an EN is present, no AN may be present, and vice versa. Fifth, in an LTR label, only characters with the Bidi properties L, EN, ES, CS, ET, ON, BN or NSM are allowed. Sixth, in an LTR label, the end of the label must be a character with Bidi property L or EN, followed by zero or more characters with Bidi property NSM.

Two guarantees follow. In a domain name consisting only of labels that satisfy the rule, the requirements of Section 3 are satisfied, and even LTR labels and pure ASCII labels have to be tested. In a domain name consisting only of LDH labels and labels that satisfy the rule, the requirements are satisfied as long as a label that starts with an ASCII digit does not come after a right-to-left label. No guarantee is given for other combinations.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule has six parts. It checks the first character, then which kinds of character may appear, then the last character, and it forbids a right-to-left label from mixing European and Arabic digits. The last character may be a combining mark, which is what lets Dhivehi and Yiddish words through.

sections.title: The Requirements the Rule Must Meet
sections.content:
This document, unlike RFC 3454, provides an explicit justification for the Bidi rule, and states a set of requirements for which it is possible to test whether the modified rule fulfils the requirement. All the text assumes that text containing the labels under consideration will be displayed using the Unicode bidirectional algorithm.

The first requirement is Label Uniqueness: no two labels, when presented in display order in the same paragraph, should have the same sequence of characters without also having the same sequence of characters in network order, both when the paragraph has LTR direction and when it has RTL direction. The second is Character Grouping: when displaying a string of labels, using the Unicode Bidi algorithm to reorder the characters for display, the characters of each label should remain grouped between the characters delimiting the labels, both in an LTR paragraph and in an RTL paragraph.

Several stronger statements were considered and rejected because they seem to be impossible to fulfil within the constraints of the Unicode bidirectional algorithm. The appearance of a label should be unaffected by its embedding context, which proved impossible even for ASCII labels. The sequence of labels should be consistent with network order, which also proved impossible. And no two domain names should be displayed the same, even under differing directionality, which was shown to be unsound: the domain name ABC.abc has display order CBA.abc in an LTR context and abc.CBA in an RTL context, while the domain name abc.ABC has display order abc.CBA in an LTR context and CBA.abc in an RTL context.
sections.plainLanguage: The document states what the rule has to achieve, so that anyone changing it can test whether the change still works. The two things it must achieve are that two different labels never end up looking identical, and that the characters of one label never get split up and mixed into the neighbouring label.

sections.title: Cases the 2003 Rule Broke
sections.content:
Dhivehi, the official language of the Maldives, is written with the Thaana script. The script displays some of the characteristics of the Arabic script, including its directional properties and the indication of vowels by diacritical marking of consonantal base characters. This marking is obligatory, and both two consecutive vowels and syllable-final consonants are indicated with unvoiced combining marks. Every Dhivehi word therefore ends with a combining mark.

The word for computer, romanized as konpeetaru, ends with U+07AA THAANA UBUFILI, whose directionality class is NSM, a Nonspacing Mark, which is not R or AL. A conformant implementation of the IDNA2003 algorithm therefore says that this is not in RandALCat and refuses to encode the string.

Yiddish is written with the Hebrew script in a fully vocalic extended form, using combining marks called points to differentiate consonants from vowels. Pointed characters can appear in word-final position, so they are also needed at the end of labels. The acronym YIVO is written with the Hebrew letters YOD YOD HIRIQ VAV VAV ALEF QAMATS, where HIRIQ and QAMATS are combining points, and U+05B8 HEBREW POINT QAMATS is NSM, which again causes the IDNA2003 algorithm to reject the string. The document also notes that all of the combined characters mentioned exist in precomposed form at separate positions in the Unicode chart, but invoking Stringprep makes the IDNA2003 algorithm reject those code points too.

Requiring that the first or last character of a string be a member of category R or AL also prohibited a string containing right-to-left characters from ending with a number. Consider the strings ALEF 5 and 5 ALEF. Displayed in an LTR context, the first will be displayed from left to right as 5 ALEF, with the 5 considered right to left because of the leading ALEF, while 5 ALEF will be displayed in exactly the same order, with the 5 taking its direction from context. Clearly only one of those should be permitted as a registered label, but barring them both seems unnecessary.
sections.plainLanguage: The document works through three real cases. Dhivehi writes its vowels as marks on the letters, so every word ends in a mark and the old rule rejected the whole language. Yiddish marks some vowels the same way, so words ending in a marked letter were rejected too. And the old rule made it impossible for a right-to-left name to end in a digit, even though that would be harmless.

sections.title: Troublesome Situations and Guidelines
sections.content:
There are situations in which labels that satisfy the rule will be displayed in a surprising fashion. The most important is the case where a label ending in a character with Bidi property AL, AN or R occurs before a label beginning with a character of Bidi property EN. In that case the number will appear to move into the label containing the right-to-left character, violating the Character Grouping requirement.

If the label that occurs after the right-to-left label itself satisfies the Bidi criterion, the requirements will be satisfied in all cases. However, the IDNABIS working group concluded that this could not be required, for several reasons: there is a large current deployment of ASCII domain names starting with digits that cannot possibly be invalidated; domain names are often constructed piecemeal, for instance by combining a string with the content of a search list, and this may occur after IDNA processing and thus in part of the code that is not IDNA-aware, making detection of the undesirable combination impossible; even if a label is registered under a safe label, there may be a DNAME with an unsafe label that points to the safe label; and wildcards create the situation where a label is valid, and can be looked up successfully, without the zone owner knowing that the label exists.

Rather than suggesting rules that disallow all such undesirable situations, the document merely warns about the possibility, and leaves it to application developers to take whatever measures they deem appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: One case is left open: a right-to-left label followed by a label that starts with a digit. The digit can appear to slide into the first label. The document does not forbid this, because there are far too many existing names that start with a digit and too many ways to build a name in pieces that the check would miss. It just warns application developers.

sections.title: Compatibility Considerations
sections.content:
Some troublesome cases arise for existing implementations when the change is introduced. An old program used to input a newly allowed label may check the input against RFC 3454, in which case some labels will not be allowed and the domain names containing them remain inaccessible. An old program asked to display a newly allowed label that checks it against RFC 3454 will perform some kind of fallback, most likely displaying the label in A-label form. And an old program that displays a newly allowed label may have separate code for the last character of a label and for the characters in the middle, so the display may be inconsistent and cause confusion. One particular example is a program that examines the last character in network order of a string to determine its directionality, rather than its first; if it finds an NSM character and tries to display the string as if it was a left-to-right string, the resulting display may be interesting, but not useful.

The editors believe these cases will have a less harmful impact in practice than continuing to deny the use of words from the languages for which these strings are necessary as IDN labels. This specification does not forbid using leading European digits in ASCII-only labels, since that would conflict with a large installed base of such labels and would increase the scope of the specification from RTL labels to all labels. Registries and private zone managers can check for this particular condition before they allow registration of any RTL label. Generally, it is best to disallow registration of any right-to-left strings in a zone where the label at the level above begins with a digit.

The text is intentionally specified strictly in terms of the Unicode Bidi properties. The determination that the conditions suffice depends on the Unicode Bidi algorithm, which is unlikely to change drastically. However, the validity of any string depends on the Bidi property values, which are not declared immutable by the Unicode Consortium, and later versions of the Unicode Standard may change the Bidi properties assigned to certain characters. The memo does not propose a solution for this problem.
sections.plainLanguage: Old software that still applies the 2003 rule will refuse some newly allowed names, and some programs that draw right-to-left text may render the new labels oddly. The authors judged that to be less harmful than keeping whole languages out of domain names. The rule is also written only in terms of Unicode direction classes, so a future Unicode version that changes a character's class could change which labels are valid.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The display behaviour of mixed-direction text can be extremely surprising to users who are not used to it. Cut and paste of a piece of text can cause the text to display differently at the destination if the destination is in another directionality context, and adding a character in one place in a text can cause characters some distance from the point of insertion to change their display position. This is not a phenomenon unique to the display of domain names.

The new IDNA protocol, and particularly these new Bidi rules, will allow some strings to be used in IDNA contexts that are not allowed today. It is possible that differences in the interpretation of labels between implementations of IDNA2003 and IDNA2008 could pose a security risk, but it is difficult to envision any specific instantiation of this. Any rational attempt to compute, for instance, a hash over an identifier processed by IDNA would use network order for its computation, and would thus be unaffected by the new rules proposed here.

While it is not believed to pose a problem, if display routines had been written with specific knowledge of the RFC 3454 IDNA prohibitions, it is possible that the potential problems noted under Backwards Compatibility Considerations could cause new kinds of confusion.
sections.plainLanguage: Mixed-direction text is confusing to read in general, not only in domain names. The new rule lets through strings that the old one rejected, so two systems could disagree about whether a name is valid, and that is where any security risk would come from. Anything that hashes a domain name uses the wire order, so hashing is unaffected.

viz.caption: The Unicode Bidi classes the rule uses

items.label: Right to left
items.desc: Most letters in non-Arabic RTL scripts.

items.label: Arabic letter
items.desc: Most letters in the Arabic script.

items.label: Arabic Number
items.desc: The Arabic-Indic numbers, but not the Extended Arabic-Indic numbers.

items.label: European Number Terminator
items.desc: Currency symbols, the hash sign, the percent sign and so on.

items.label: Common Number Separator
items.desc: Full stop, comma, slash, colon and similar.

items.label: Nonspacing Mark
items.desc: Most combining accents, including the marks that end Dhivehi and Yiddish words.

items.label: Boundary Neutral
items.desc: Control characters such as ZWNJ and ZWJ.

items.label: Other Neutrals
items.desc: The at sign, ampersand, parentheses, middle dot and similar.

viz.caption: The six conditions of the Bidi rule

items.title: 1. First character
items.text: It must have Bidi property L, R or AL. R or AL makes the label RTL; L makes it LTR.

items.title: 2. Characters allowed in an RTL label
items.text: Only R, AL, AN, EN, ES, CS, ET, ON, BN or NSM.

items.title: 3. Last characters of an RTL label
items.text: R, AL, EN or AN, followed by zero or more NSM.

items.title: 4. Digits in an RTL label
items.text: If an EN is present, no AN may be present, and vice versa.

items.title: 5. Characters allowed in an LTR label
items.text: Only L, EN, ES, CS, ET, ON, BN or NSM.

items.title: 6. Last characters of an LTR label
items.text: L or EN, followed by zero or more NSM.

viz.caption: The cases that pushed the 2003 rule to be replaced

cells: Every word ends in a combining mark, so every word was rejected as an IDN label.
Pointed characters can end a word, and the acronym YIVO ends in a combining point, so it was rejected.
Right-to-left label ending in a number
A string with right-to-left characters was not allowed to end with a number.
